California NORML’s Proposed "Friendly Amendment" To Proposition 215
Sent to Senator Vasconcellos

From Dale H. Gieringer, Ph.D.
Coordinator, California NORML

Here is California NORML’s official testimony to the Vasconcellos hearing on medical marijuana distribution. As you will see, it is aimed to circumvent the regulatory model that Steve Kubby has rightly criticized.
See

May 11, 1998

Sen. Vasconcellos, Chair
State Senate Public Safety Committee
State Capitol 4061
Sacramento CA 95814

Dear Sen. Vasconcellos:

As one of the organizing sponsors of the 1996 Compassionate Use Initiative, California NORML offers the following comments for your committee’s consideration concerning medical marijuana distribution.

Proposition 215 deliberately did not propose a distribution system for medical marijuana.

Unfortunately, the federal government has failed to address this mandate in a constructive and timely manner. Instead, it has refused to reschedule marijuana for medical use until it has been approved through the FDA new drug approval process. It is a sad commentary on the government’s lack of responsiveness that 18 months after the election, not a single FDA efficacy review is underway (Dr. Donald Abrams’ study having been downgraded to a safety review).
See

Barring a change in federal policy, a minimum of 3-4 years would seem necessary for marijuana to be rescheduled.

In the meantime, the only feasible distribution system will be through private agencies such as cannabis patients’ cooperatives or "clubs." Distribution by public entities appears legally unworkable so long as cannabis remains in Schedule 1, although public agencies might legally perform the useful function of overseeing and regulating medical cannabis distribution. (It is possible that the impending federal lawsuit against the cannabis clubs will render even private medical distribution legally unfeasible, although the legitimacy and efficacy of federal authority over intrastate medical use seems dubious in light of the passage of Proposition 215.)

Proposition 215 was written with the intent of legitimizing some form of patients’ cooperatives by way of the caregivers’ provision. Unfortunately, the vagueness of the wording has leant itself to various interpretations, leading to considerable confusion. The result has been a kind of legal anarchy, in which all kinds of clubs, cooperatives, and providers have undertaken to distribute and produce medical marijuana, some with, and others without, the approval of local authorities.

From this mixed bag, the best providers have emerged with strong support from their communities for having responsibly served the needs of thousands of seriously ill patients covered by Prop. 215. Others have floundered or been forced to close by law enforcement under the Health & Safety Code provisions concerning marijuana, which are unfortunately the only legal device now available for regulating medical cannabis.
See

Experience has shown that well-run patient cooperatives offer benefits to both public health and safety, affording patients a safe, reliable, accountable source of medicine and relieving them of the need to rely on illicit street traffickers. Cannabis clubs also offer distinct therapeutic benefits to users not available through conventional pharmacy distribution Many club members are socially isolated, depressed, or suffer psychological or substance abuse problems that may be alleviated through social support. For these patients clubs can provide unique therapeutic benefits, as explained in an article by Harvard psychiatrist Dr. Lester Grinspoon and a forthcoming study of San Francisco cannabis club clients by Dr. Harvey Feldman and Jerry Mandel to be published in the Journal of Psychoactive Drugs.

RECOMMENDATIONS:

(1) Allow for the legal distribution of medicinal cannabis through legally registered patients’ cooperatives, organized on a not-for-profit basis. Laws against transportation, paraphernalia, maintaining a drug house, etc., should likewise be modified to exempt legal cooperatives and their clients.

(2) Establish a voluntary patient identification system with tight safeguards for patient privacy in order to reduce the current confusion and uncertainty surrounding enforcement of Prop. 215. Realizing that many patients, especially PWA’s, are understandably reluctant to register, and that mandatory registration is inconsistent with the language of Prop. 215, we believe this system should be voluntary. However, patients would be induced to register by the incentives of (1) greater legal protection from arrest and (2) certified eligibility to obtain medicine from co-ops.

For the protection of all parties, identification should be certified through a public agency. The Arcata ordinance provides a good model here. See
Most Governments In California Have Flunked The Test Of Implementation Of Prop 215 – Orange County Register
Alternatively, if a state medical marijuana research program is established, this would afford a logical facility for patient registration.

(3) Permit local governments to regulate cannabis cooperatives through appropriate ordinances and revoke or deny registrations for improper conduct.

(4) Encourage cooperatives to grow cannabis for themselves rather than purchase from black market suppliers. Designated cultivation sites allow for better inspection and quality control, and avoid problems associated with the illicit market. Use of police-confiscated cannabis should be avoided, as illicit supplies are of suspect quality and subject to contamination from mold, pesticides, etc. High-grade, medicinal quality cannabis is already currently being produced by the quasi-legal gardens now supplying the clubs, though in insufficient quantities. California NORML has been helping sponsor laboratory tests of these products, preliminary results of which indicate that they are of greatly superior medical quality to the cannabis currently provided for human research by the federal government through NIDA.
